parts.problemMd:
This question is about gases in the atmosphere.

A teacher uses this apparatus to determine the percentage of oxygen in air.

![Diagram of a setup with two gas syringes connected to a tube containing pieces of copper wire. One gas syringe contains 50 cm³ of air, and the other is empty.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-modular-24-unit-2/inorganic-chemistry/atmospheric-gases/assets/001-diagram-of-a-setup-with-two-gas-syringes-connect.png)

The teacher heats the copper wire strongly and passes the air in the syringe from one side to the other.

She then lets the apparatus cool down and she measures the volume of air in the syringe.

i) State the appearance of the copper wire after heating.

[1]

ii) Write an equation for the reaction between copper and oxygen.

[1]

iii) Explain why the teacher leaves the apparatus to cool down before taking a reading of the volume.

[1]

iv) Explain why the teacher uses copper wire rather than a piece of copper.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) After heating, the copper wire is:
> 
> - Black (solid) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction between copper and oxygen is:
> 
> - 2Cu + O<sub>2</sub> → 2CuO **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The apparatus needs to cool down before taking a reading of the volume because:
> 
> - To allow the gas to cool to room temperature 
> **OR**
> Air expands when heated / contracts when cooled **[1 mark]**
> 
> iv) Copper wire is used rather than a piece of copper because:
> 
> - Copper wire has a larger surface area **[1 mark]**
> - So, the rate of reaction is faster **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> i) Examiner reports often show that students are uncertain about the colour changes for copper compounds. It is worth memorising the key ones:
> 
> - Copper metal: pink-brown / orange-brown
> - Copper(II) oxide: black
> - Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate: white
> - Hydrated copper(II) sulfate: blue
> 
> iii) Examiner reports talk about how a minority of students realise that the apparatus needs to be left to cool (to room temperature). This is because the volume of a gas changes with temperature; it expands when heated and contracts when cooled.
> 
> iv) When a question asks "why" one form of a solid is used over another (e.g., wire vs. a lump, or powder vs. large chips), the answer is almost always about surface area and its effect on the rate of reaction.

parts.problemMd: Calculate the expected volume of gas in the syringe at room temperature.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the expected volume of gas in the syringe at room temperature:

**Method 1: Calculating the volume of gas that remains**

- Calculate the percentage of other gases in air:

% other gases = 100% - 21% = 79% **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the volume of these unreacted gases:

volume remaining = 50 cm<sup>3</sup> × $\frac{79}{100}$ **[1 mark]**

volume remaining = **39.5 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

**Method 2: Calculating the volume of oxygen that reacts**

- State the percentage of oxygen:

oxygen = 21% **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the volume of oxygen that reacts with the copper:

volume of oxygen = 50 cm<sup>3</sup> × $\frac{21}{100}$ = 10.5 cm<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Subtract the volume of reacted oxygen from the initial volume:

final volume = 50 - 10.5

final volume = **39.5 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> A correct answer of 39.5 with no working scores 3 marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> To answer this question, you must recall the approximate percentage of oxygen in the air (~21%).
> 
> You can:
> 
> - Either calculate the volume of the gases that **do not react** (79% of the total)
> - Or calculate the volume of oxygen that **does react** (21% of the total) and subtract it from the starting volume
> 
> Both methods will give you the same correct answer.

parts.problemMd:
The teacher measures the volume of the syringe at the end of the experiment and records the volume as 42 cm<sup>3</sup>.

Give one reason why this was not the expected result.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One reason why this was not the expected result is:
> 
> - The reaction was incomplete / did not go to completion **OR** Not all the oxygen was used up **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In this question, you have to use the answer to the previous part to come up with the correct explanation. If your previous answer was less than the expected volume, you might still get credit based on your answer.
> 
> To answer this question, you must first compare the experimental result with your calculated answer from part (b).
> 
> - **Experimental result:** 42 cm<sup>3</sup>
> - **Calculated (expected) result:** 39.5 cm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> The experimental volume is **higher** than expected. This means that **less oxygen was removed** from the air than predicted. The most likely reason for this is that the reaction was incomplete, and some of the oxygen did not react with the copper.
> 
> If the volume was less than expected, then you could say that air leaks were responsible.

parts.problemMd:

Which is the correct statement about combustion?

|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **B** | During the combustion of sulfur, a blue flame is observed and a colourless, poisonous gas is produced |

parts.solutionMd:

- **B** / During the combustion of sulfur, a blue flame is observed and a colourless, poisonous gas is produced; **[1 mark]**

- *The correct answer is **B** because aulfur reacts with oxygen during a combustion reaction forming sulfur dioxide*

- *C** is incorrect as combustion reactions are all exothermic as heat is released*
- *D** is incorrect as water (not hydrogen peroxide, H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*2*</sub>*) is produced during the combustion of hydrogen, 2H*<sub>*2 *</sub>*+ O*<sub>*2 *</sub>*→ 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*

- Volume of oxygen = 20 cm<sup>3</sup>; [1 mark]
- Total volume = 253 cm<sup>3</sup>; [1 mark]
- Percentage of oxygen = $\frac{20}{253}\times100$ = 7.9%;  **[1 mark]**

iii) One reason why the calculated percentage of oxygen in the mixture may not be accurate is:

- There may be a leak (in the equipment) 
**OR **
The temperature was not the same for all readings 
**OR **
The equipment was not left to cool (to room temperature); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *For part (ii)*

  - *If the volume of oxygen and / or the total volume are incorrect, the subsequent marks can still be scored by error carried forward*
  - *A correct answer of 7.9% without working scores all 3 marks*
- *The volume of oxygen is the amount that the results have decreased by, i.e. 78 → 58 = 20 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *
- *The total volume is the 175 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of the glass tube and connecting tubes plus the initial 78 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* in syringe A*
- *A common mistake with this calculation is to get answers over 100%, which is not possible*

  - *If this happens, check the values you are using and check that you have them the correct way up in the division calculation*
- *The results would not be accurate because of issues with the equipment: *

  - *As you are dealing with gases and have equipment with multiple connections, there are likely to be leaks in the equipment*
  - *It cannot be because not all of the oxygen has reacted - all of the oxygen was shown to have reacted in part (i)*

parts.problemMd:
A student uses this apparatus to investigate the effect of heat on different solid metal carbonates.

![1cr-q5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-modular-24-unit-2/inorganic-chemistry/atmospheric-gases/assets/002-1cr-q5.png)

This is the student’s method:

- Use a spatula to put some metal carbonate in the boiling tube
- Fit the delivery tube into position
- Pour some limewater into the test tube
- Start a timer and immediately begin to heat the metal carbonate
- Record the time when a change first occurs in the limewater

The student repeats the method using different metal carbonates.

When a metal carbonate is heated a reaction sometimes occurs. The equation for the reaction is:

metal carbonate → metal oxide + carbon dioxide

State the name given to this type of reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
The name given to this type of reaction is:

- (Thermal) decomposition; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The metal carbonate is broken down or decomposed into metal oxide and carbon dioxide*
- *This decomposition requires heat*
- *Therefore, the reaction is thermal decomposition*

parts.problemMd:
State two variables that the student should control in this investigation.

1. ........................................... 2. ...........................................
parts.solutionMd:
Two variables that the student should control in this investigation:

Any **two** from:

- Use the same amount of metal carbonate;** [1 mark]**
- Use the same sized pieces/surface area; **[1 mark]**
- Use the same volume of limewater; **[1 mark]**
- Use the same size flame / distance of flame from boiling tube; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *These are called control or controlled variables*

  - *You could use 'mass' instead of amount of metal carbonate*
  - *You could use 'amount' instead of volume of limewater, although this is not ideal as volume is more specific*

parts.problemMd: Suggest why bubbles appear in the limewater immediately after heating has started but before there is any change to the metal carbonate.
parts.solutionMd:
Why bubbles appear in the limewater immediately after heating has started but before there is any change to the metal carbonate:

- The bubbles come from the air inside the apparatus expanding as it gets heated; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *When the test-tube is heated, the first thing that will happen is that any gases present will spread out even further*
- *This causes some bubbling to be seen*
- *But, no change is seen in the limewater because these first bubbles are air*

parts.problemMd: Explain the purpose of limewater in this investigation.
parts.solutionMd:
The purpose of limewater in this investigation:

- The limewater turns cloudy when carbon dioxide is present; **[1 mark]**
- Showing that the metal carbonate has decomposed; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *The most common incorrect or incomplete answer to this question is about the limewater testing for carbon dioxide*
- *But, this is being used as a way to check that the metal carbonate has decomposed*

parts.problemMd:
The table shows some of the results for the student’s investigation.

| **Metal carbonate** | **Colour change of solid ** | **Time taken for any** **change in limewater** |
|---|---|---|
| calcium carbonate | remains white | 90 seconds |
| sodium carbonate | remains white | no change |
| copper(II) carbonate |   | 50 seconds |

i) State the colour change that occurs for copper(II) carbonate.

from ...................................... to ...................................

(2)

ii) Give a chemical equation for this reaction of copper(II) carbonate.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i)   The colour change that occurs for copper(II) carbonate.

- Green; **[1 mark]**
- (to) black; **[1 mark]**

ii)  A chemical equation for this reaction of copper(II) carbonate:

- CuCO<sub>3</sub> →  CuO + CO<sub>2</sub> ; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *You can be expected to know the colour of copper carbonate and copper oxide*

  - *Examiners often comment about how the colours of certain compounds are not well known*
- *Remember: **Metal carbonate → metal oxide + carbon dioxide*

  - *MCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* → MO + CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* *

parts.problemMd:
f) There is a relationship between the position of a metal in the reactivity series and how easily the metal carbonate reacts when heated.

I) Use the student’s results and your own knowledge to deduce this relationship.

(2)

ii) State how you should extend the investigation to see if your deduction is correct.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i)  Deduce this relationship using the student's results and your knowledge:

- The further down or lower the metal is in the reactivity series; **[1 mark]**
- The more easily the metal carbonate decomposes; **[1 mark]**

ii)  How you should extend the investigation to see if your deduction is correct:

- Repeat the experiment using different metal carbonates; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *You can also get credit in part i) for saying the shorter the time it takes for the carbonate to decompose*
- *Reverse arguments are also credited, e.g. the more reactive the metal the harder the metal carbonate is to decompose*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about determining the percentage composition by volume of a mixture of three gases, oxygen, carbon dioxide and argon in air.

Two experiments are done to determine the percentage composition by volume of oxygen.

In experiment 1, a student connects a gas syringe to a conical flask filled with iron filings. The diagram shows the apparatus the student uses.

![2-3-3a-h-a](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-modular-24-unit-2/inorganic-chemistry/atmospheric-gases/assets/007-2-3-3a-h-a.png)

i) Give two changes the student needs to make to the apparatus in experiment 1 to find the percentage by volume of oxygen in a sample of air.

(2)

In experiment 2, two 100 cm<sup>3</sup> gas syringes are connected to a reaction tube containing copper powder. The sample of air is passed over hot copper oxide. The diagram shows the apparatus that is used.

![2-3-3a-h-b](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-modular-24-unit-2/inorganic-chemistry/atmospheric-gases/assets/008-2-3-3a-h-b.png)

ii) Explain why both syringes should not be filled with 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) Two changes that the student needs to make to the apparatus to find the percentage by volume of oxygen in a sample of air are:

- Use wet iron filings;** [1 mark]**
- Use a gas syringe filled with air / set to 100 cm<sup>3</sup>  **OR **Not use a gas syringe with no air inside / at 0 cm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**

ii) Both syringes should not be filled with 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of air because:

Any of the following linked pairs:

- When the apparatus is heated, the air / gases will spread out; **[1 mark]**
- Which can cause the syringes to open; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- When the air / gas is pushed from one syringe to the other syringe, the syringe will open; **[1 mark]**
- As 100 cm<sup>3</sup> syringes cannot hold (over) 200 cm<sup>3</sup> of air; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *For part (i)*

  - *The reaction that will happen is the rusting of iron*
  - *The oxygen in the conical flask will react very slowly with the iron filings*
  
    - *Adding water / making the iron filings wet will make the reaction happen quicker / on a more appropriate timescale*
  - *To be able to calculate the percentage by volume of oxygen, you will need a measurement of how much oxygen has been removed from the air*
  
    - *This means that you need to have the gas syringe filled with 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of air*
    - *This allows you to see how much oxygen has reacted from the air*
- *For part (ii)*

  - *One syringe should be full and the other empty*
  - *This allows you to pass the air over the hot copper powder, from one syringe to the other*
  - *As the reaction proceeds, the total volume of air in the syringes will decrease as the oxygen reacts*

parts.problemMd:
When the apparatus in experiment 2 is set up correctly, the mixture of gases is passed over the hot copper powder.

The total volume of the mixture of gases in the syringes at the start is 76 cm<sup>3</sup>.

The total volume of the mixture of gases in the syringes at the end is 64 cm<sup>3</sup>.

i) Calculate the percentage by volume of oxygen in the mixture of gases.

(2)

ii) Explain how the answer to part (i) suggests that all of the oxygen has not reacted.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The percentage by volume of oxygen in the mixture of gases is:

- Volume of oxygen = 12 cm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Percentage of oxygen = 15.8%; **[1 mark]**

ii) The answer to part (i) suggests that all of the oxygen has not reacted because:

- The percentage of oxygen in the air is roughly 20 / 21%; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The volume of oxygen that reacts is 76 - 64 = 12 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *
- *Therefore, the percentage of oxygen in the air is* $\frac{12}{76}\times100$* = 15.8%*
- *The percentage of oxygen in the air would be expected to be around 20 / 21%*
- *Since the percentage of oxygen in the air according to this experiment is less than 20 / 21%, it suggests that not all of the oxygen has reacted*

parts.problemMd:
To determine the percentage of carbon dioxide in the air, the student suggests adapting the apparatus in experiment 2.

They suggest replacing the reaction tube containing copper powder with a conical flask containing limewater, as shown.

![2-3-3c-h-per-cent-of-co2-in-air](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-modular-24-unit-2/inorganic-chemistry/atmospheric-gases/assets/009-2-3-3c-h-per-cent-of-co2-in-air.png)

Explain why this experiment will not show the presence of carbon dioxide and give two reasons why this experiment will not allow the percentage of carbon dioxide in the air to be determined.
parts.solutionMd:
This experiment will not show the presence of carbon dioxide and will not allow the percentage of carbon dioxide in the air to be determined because:

Not showing the presence of carbon dioxide:

- The air / gas is not bubbled through the limewater **OR **The air / gas does not pass through the limewater **OR **The left-hand tube is not in the limewater / does not reach the limewater; **[1 mark]**
- So, the limewater will not turn cloudy (to confirm the presence of carbon dioxide);** [1 mark]**

Not allowing the determination of the percentage of carbon dioxide: Any **two** of the following:

- The carbon dioxide (in the air / gas) is not removed / does not react with the limewater;** [1 mark]**
- The expected percentage of carbon dioxide (in the air / gas) is too small / only 0.04%;** [1 mark]**
- The divisions / scale on the gas syringes is too large (for meaningful results) **OR **The gas syringes are too big / large; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Remember:** The chemical test for carbon dioxide is that the gas is bubbled through limewater, which turns cloudy*

  - *The apparatus in this experiment does not allow the gas to bubble through the limewater*
  - *This means that the carbon dioxide does not react with the limewater*
  - *Therefore, there can be no positive test for carbon dioxide*
- *The syringes used in this experiment are 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* and the expected percentage of carbon dioxide in the air is around 0.04%*

  - *If the total volume of air in both gas syringes, the conical flask and the tubes was 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>*, then you would expect to see a decrease in the total volume of 0.04 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *
  - *The divisions / scale on the 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* gas syringes will be too large to accurately measure this change in volume *

parts.problemMd:
The percentage by volume of argon cannot be determined directly because it is very unreactive.

Explain why argon is extremely unreactive.
parts.solutionMd:
Argon is extremely unreactive because:

- Argon has a full / complete outer shell of electrons **OR **Argon has eight outer shell electrons.** [1 mark]**
- So, it does not lose or gain (or share) electrons;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Remember: **The lack of reactivity in the Group 0 elements is because they have a full outer shell of electrons*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the combustion of fuels and atmospheric pollution.

Methane is a common fuel that can be combusted.

CH<sub>4</sub> (g) + 2O<sub>2</sub> (g) → CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Calculate the mass of methane that is required to produce 50.0 g of carbon dioxide.
parts.solutionMd:
The volume of methane required to produce 50.0 g of carbon dioxide is:

- Moles of carbon dioxide = 1.137 **AND **Moles of methane = 1.137;** [1 mark]**
- Mass of methane = 18.2 (g); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *First, you need to calculate the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of carbon dioxide and methane*

  - *Carbon dioxide, CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* = 12 + (2 x 16) = 44*
  - *Methane, CH*<sub>*4*</sub>* = 12 + (4 x 1) = 16*
- *The main calculation part of this question uses variations of the moles =* $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$ *equation*
- *Then, you need to calculate the moles of carbon dioxide *

  - $\frac{50.0}{44}$ *= 1.137*
- *Since 1 mole of methane reacts to form 1 mole of carbon dioxide, the number of moles of methane is also 1.137*
- *Finally, you calculate the mass of methane*

  - *1.137 x 16 = 18.2 g*

parts.problemMd:
An experiment is set up to show the products of combustion for methane.

![2-3-4b-h-products-of-combustion-incorrect-set-up](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-modular-24-unit-2/inorganic-chemistry/atmospheric-gases/assets/004-2-3-4b-h-products-of-combustion-incorrect-set-up.png)

i) Write a chemical equation for the reaction that occurs in the limewater as it gives a positive test for one of the combustion products.

(1)

ii) The cobalt chloride paper tests for the other combustion product. Explain why the set-up of this apparatus does not prove that this combustion product is produced.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The chemical equation for the reaction that occurs in the limewater is:

- Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub> → CaCO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O;** [1 mark]**

ii) The set-up of this apparatus does not prove that this combustion product is produced because:

- Cobalt chloride tests for water **OR **Cobalt chloride changes <u>from blue to pink</u> with water; **[1 mark]**
- It can change due to the water from limewater / the limewater solution / Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq); **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Limewater is calcium hydroxide with the chemical formula Ca(OH)*<sub>*2*</sub>* (aq)*

  - *This reacts with carbon dioxide to give a cloudy / milky / white precipitate of calcium carbonate, CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* (s), and water*
  
    - *Ca(OH)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *This equation requires no balancing, which explains why part (i) is only for one mark*
- *Cobalt chloride paper is blue when dry *

  - *This colour changes to pink when it is wet*
  - *The gases produced from the combustion of methane are carbon dioxide and water, which pass through the apparatus*
  - *Since the gases pass into the limewater first, it is likely that the water would condense inside the limewater solution*
  - *Even if the water did not condense in the limewater, the gases that pass through to the cobalt chloride paper have passed through the limewater solution*
  
    - *This means that the cobalt chloride paper could turn pink due to the combustion product **OR** due to the water from the limewater solution*

parts.problemMd:
Fossil fuels are burned in car engines releasing carbon dioxide and other gases. Rainwater is acidic because carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form carbonic acid along with other acidic pollutant gases, such as nitrogen dioxide, dissolving in the water.

i) Give the name of the acid that forms when nitrogen dioxide dissolves in water.

(1)

ii) Explain how nitrogen dioxide is produced in a car engine if there are no nitrogen-based impurities in fossil fuels?

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The name of the acid that forms when nitrogen dioxide dissolves in water is:

- Nitric acid / HNO<sub>3</sub> **OR **Nitrous acid / HNO<sub>2</sub>;** [1 mark]**

ii) Nitrogen dioxide is produced in a car engine when there are no nitrogen-based impurities in fossil fuels because:

- Fossil fuels are burned / combusted at high temperatures (in a car engine); **[1 mark]**
- So, nitrogen (from the air) reacts with oxygen (from the air) **OR **N<sub>2</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO<sub>2</sub> **AND **the nitrogen comes from the air; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The most common answer to this question is nitric acid*

  - *NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O → HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>* (nitric acid)*
- *The atmosphere is approximately 78% nitrogen*

  - *This means that the air that is taken into a car engine during combustion can react*
  - *Although nitrogen is relatively unreactive, at the high temperatures inside a car engine it will react with oxygen to form nitrogen oxides which are also responsible for acid rain*

parts.problemMd: Explain how reducing the amount of sulfur in fossil fuels reduces the erosion of limestone.
parts.solutionMd:
Reducing the amount of sulfur in fossil fuels reduces the erosion of limestone because:

- Sulfur reacts with oxygen / burns / combusts to form sulfur dioxide / SO<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Reducing sulfur in fossil fuels means that less sulfur dioxide is emitted; **[1 mark]**
- Which means there is less acid rain to react with limestone; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *This question tests your knowledge of how the products of combustion of impurities cause pollution and the effects*
- *Sulfur forms sulfur dioxide, which is linked to acid rain*
- *The sulfurous / sulfuric acid formed reacts with limestone as it is a carbonate*

  - *Metal carbonate + acid → metal salt + carbon dioxide + water*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the percentage of oxygen in the air.

The percentage of oxygen in the air can be determined by observing the formation of hydrated iron(III) oxide.

Write the balanced chemical equation for the formation of iron(III) oxide from iron.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced chemical equation for the formation of iron(III) oxide from iron is:

4Fe + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>

- Correct chemical formulae;** [1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Careful:** The question asks for the formation of iron(III) oxide, **not** hydrated iron(III) oxide*
- *The chemical formula of iron(III) oxide is Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>

  - *The Roman numeral tells you that the iron is Fe*<sup>*3+*</sup>* *
  - *Oxygen is O*<sup>*2–*</sup>
  - *To balance the charges, you need two irons and three oxygens *
  - *This gives the formula Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
- *Iron reacts with oxygen to form iron(III) oxide*

  - *Fe + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
- *There are two oxygen atoms on the left-hand side and three oxygen atoms on the right-hand side*

  - *So, working with six oxygen atoms on both sides will allow us to begin balancing the equation*
  - *Fe + **3**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
- *There are now four iron atoms on the right-hand side and only one on the left-hand side*

  - *This can be solved by using four iron atoms on the left-hand side*
  - *4**Fe + **3**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>* *

parts.problemMd:
A student sets up this apparatus to observe the formation of hydrated iron(III) oxide.

![2-3-5b-h-per-cent-of-air-using-iron-filings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-modular-24-unit-2/inorganic-chemistry/atmospheric-gases/assets/011-2-3-5b-h-per-cent-of-air-using-iron-filings.png)

The reading on the syringe is recorded at the start of the experiment. The apparatus is then left for a week before the reading on the syringe is recorded again.

The table shows the initial reading of the syringe.

| syringe reading at start / cm<sup>3</sup> | 100 |
|---|---|
| syringe reading at end / cm<sup>3</sup> |   |
| volume of oxygen used / cm<sup>3</sup> |   |

The atmosphere is comprised of 20% oxygen. Complete the table to show the expected results.
parts.solutionMd:
To complete the table for the expected results:

| syringe reading at start / cm<sup>3</sup> | 100 |
|---|---|
| syringe reading at end / cm<sup>3</sup> | 59 |
| volume of oxygen used / cm<sup>3</sup> | 41 |

- Total volume of air = 205 (cm<sup>3</sup>) **AND **Volume of oxygen used = 41 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Syringe reading at end = 59 cm<sup>3</sup>;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Careful:** The table and gas syringe in the diagram are actually distractions to the main calculation*

  - *Many students will try to read the value from the gas syringe*
  
    - *It does appear to be around 52 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* which would give a volume of 48 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen used*
    - *But, the image is not clear enough for you to be able to do this*
  - *Some students will rush to a final syringe reading of 80 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* and the volume of oxygen used as 20 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *
  
    - *This is because the initial syringe reading is 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *
    - *If 20% of this is oxygen, then 20 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* will be used giving the final syringe reading as 80 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
    - *This is incorrect as it does not account for the air in the delivery tube and conical flask*
- *You have to calculate 20% of the **total** volume of air in the apparatus to work out how much oxygen will be used up*

  - *Total volume = 100 + 5 + 100 = 205 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *
  - *20% of the total volume =* $\frac{205}{100}\times20$ *OR **205 x 0.2 = 41 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *
- *This is the volume of oxygen that is used up and will cause the reading on the syringe to decrease by 41 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *

  - *100 - 41 = 59 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *

parts.problemMd:
A student completes a second experiment.

The diagram shows the readings on the student's experiment.

![2-3-5c-h-syringe-readings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-modular-24-unit-2/inorganic-chemistry/atmospheric-gases/assets/012-2-3-5c-h-syringe-readings.png)

The student completes their results table, as shown, to calculate that the percentage of oxygen in the air is 21.5%.

| syringe reading at start / cm<sup>3</sup> | 84 |
|---|---|
| syringe reading at end / cm<sup>3</sup> | 40 |
| volume of oxygen used / cm<sup>3</sup> | 44 |

Identify the error that the student has made and calculate the correct percentage of oxygen in the air.
parts.solutionMd:
The error that the student has made is:

- The syringe reading at the start is not 84 (cm<sup>3</sup>) **OR **The syringe reading at the start should be 76 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

To calculate the correct percentage of oxygen in the air:

- Volume of oxygen used = 36 (cm<sup>3</sup>);** [1 mark]**
- Percentage of oxygen in the air = 17.6(%); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *It is not enough to say that the syringe reading at the start is wrong*

  - *You have the information available and should be giving an answer using the specific values shown*
- *The student has made the common mistake of misreading the value on the syringe at the start of the experiment *

  - *Each division on the syringe represents 2 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *
  - *But the scale is decreasing from left to right, so the reading should be 80 - 4 = 76 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* *
  - *This mistake is even easier to make / miss, when you are given the values*
- *This means that the calculation for the percentage of oxygen in the air will be:*

  - $\frac{36}{205}\times100$ *= 17.6%*

parts.problemMd:
Another set of experiments featured changes to the apparatus.

i) Explain how the use of dry iron filings would affect the calculated percentage of oxygen in the air.

(3)

ii) Explain how leaving the apparatus in a warm place for 1 week would affect the calculated percentage of oxygen in the air.

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
i) How the use of dry iron filings would affect the calculated percentage of oxygen in the air:

- The percentage (of oxygen in the air) would be lower / less / decrease; **[1 mark]**

Explanation:

- Rusting requires water; **[1 mark]**
- So, less / no oxygen would react **OR **So, the volume of oxygen used would decrease / be less; **[1 mark]**

ii) How leaving the apparatus in a warm place for 1 week would affect the calculated percentage of oxygen in the air:

- The percentage (of oxygen in the air) would not change **OR **There will be no effect;** [1 mark]**

Explanation:

- The reaction would proceed / happen quicker / faster; **[1 mark]**
- But, the overall volume of oxygen used up will still be the same as the iron filings are in excess; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *These explain the effect type questions are always considered more challenging, with examiners often commenting on how poor the general standard of answers was*
- *Take your time to identify what the change is, the immediate effect on the rusting reaction and then the effect on the calculated percentage of oxygen in the air*
- *For part (i)*

mass of oxygen = .............................. g
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the mass of oxygen required to react with 32 g of methane:

Method 1:

- Moles of methane: $\frac{32}{16}$ = 2;** [1 mark]**
- Mass of oxygen: (32 x 2 x 2) = 128 (g); **[1 mark]** *A final answer of 128  scores both marks*

Method 2:

- 16 g of methane needs 64 g of oxygen;** [1 mark]**
- Therefore, 32 g of methane needs 128 g of oxygen**[1 mark] ***A final answer of 128  scores both marks*

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *From the equation, 1 mole of methane reacts with 2 moles of oxygen*
- *32 g of methane is 2 moles of methane*
- *2 moles of methane will, therefore, require 4 moles of oxygen*
- *4 moles of oxygen has a mass of (4 x 32) = 128 g*

parts.solutionMd:
i) The mass of (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> produced by heating is:

- Moles of H<sub>2</sub>O = $\frac{5.40}{18}$ **OR **Moles of H<sub>2</sub>O = 0.3; **[1 mark] **
- x = $\frac{0.3}{0.0125}$;* ***[1 mark] **
- x = 24;** [1 mark] **

**[Total: 6 marks] **

- *You can calculate the value of x by doing an empirical formula type calculation*

  - *You swap:*
  
    - *The elements for the salt ((NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*.Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*(SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*<sub>*3*</sub>*) and water (H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O)*

|---|---|---|
| Value | 6.65 | 5.40 |
| *M*<sub>r</sub> | 532 | 18 |
| $\frac{\mathrm{Value}}{M_{r}}$ | $\frac{6.65}{532}$ = 0.0125 | $\frac{5.40}{18}$ = 0.3 |
| Ratio (divide by the smallest answer) | $\frac{0.0125}{0.0125}$ = 1 | $\frac{0.3}{0.0125}$ = 24 |
- *You now have the ratio of (NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*.Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*(SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*<sub>*3*</sub>* to H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O *

- *Therefore, x = 24*

parts.problemMd:
A scientist finds an unlabelled bottle on a shelf.

She thinks the bottle contains a solution of ammonium sulfate, (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

Describe tests the scientist could do to show that the solution is ammonium sulfate.
parts.solutionMd:
The tests that the scientist could do to show that the solution is ammonium sulfate are:

Test for ammonium ions:

- Add sodium hydroxide (solution) / other hydroxide solution **OR **Warm with sodium hydroxide (solution); **[1 mark]**
- Test the gas with (damp) (red) litmus <u>paper</u> / (damp) universal indicator <u>paper</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Litmus turns blue  / Universal indicator turns blue / purple (if ammonium ions are present); **[1 mark]**

Test for sulfate ions:

- Add (dilute hydrochloric / nitric) acid **OR **Acidify (the solution);** [1 mark]**
- Add barium chloride (solution) / barium nitrate (solution); **[1 mark]**
- A white precipitate forms (if sulfate ions are present); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *You need to know the various chemical tests*
- *The test for the ammonium ion is typically answered poorly*

  - *Lots of students fail to add that it is the gas being tested*
- *The test for the sulfate ion, using barium chloride more often than barium nitrate, is usually answered well*

parts.problemMd:
Ammonium sulfate is often used as a fertiliser.

It is prepared by reacting ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>) with sulfuric acid (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>).

i) Name the type of reaction that occurs between ammonia and sulfuric acid.

(1)

ii) Write a chemical equation for the reaction of ammonia with sulfuric acid.

(1)

iii) Draw a dot‐and‐cross diagram to show the bonding in a molecule of ammonia.

Show outer electrons only.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The type of reaction that occurs between ammonia and sulfuric acid is:

- Neutralisation **OR** Acid-base / acid-alkali;** [1 mark]**

ii) The chemical equation for the reaction of ammonia with sulfuric acid is:

2NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>;** [1 mark] **

iii) The dot‐and‐cross diagram to show the bonding in a molecule of ammonia is:

![Ammonia dot cross diagram](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-modular-24-unit-2/inorganic-chemistry/chemical-tests/assets/004-ammonia-dot-cross-diagram.jpeg)

- 3 bonding pairs (1 pair between nitrogen and each hydrogen); **[1 mark]**
- Rest of the molecule correct; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Sulfuric acid is obviously an acid and ammonia is a base, so they will react in a neutralisation reaction to form ammonium sulfate*
- *To draw the ammonia molecule:*

  - *Nitrogen is in Group 5 so it needs to share 3 electrons to be considered complete*
  - *Place the nitrogen atom in the centre*
  - *Place the 3 hydrogen atoms in the south, east and west positions with shells overlapping*
  - *Add a pair of electrons to each overlap*
  
    - *Remember:** Hydrogen atoms are full / complete with 2 electrons*
  - *Add the lone pair for nitrogen in the north position*
  - *Check that the nitrogen atom now has 8 electrons*

parts.problemMd:
A student is given a mixture of two white solid compounds, and a colourless solution containing the same two compounds.

The student is told that one of the compounds is a halide and that the other compound is a carbonate.

Give two reasons why the student should know, without doing any tests, that one of the compounds cannot be copper(II) carbonate.
parts.solutionMd:
Two reasons why the student should know, without doing any tests, that one of the compounds cannot be copper(II) carbonate are:

- Copper(II) carbonate is green;** [1 mark]**
- Copper(II) carbonate is insoluble / not soluble **OR **Copper(II) carbonate does not form a solution;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *You can be expected to know that:*

  - *Copper(II) carbonate is green*
  
    - *Statements about it not being white or being a different colour are ignored*
  - *Only sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates are soluble*

parts.problemMd: Describe tests the student could do to show that the mixture contains potassium carbonate and potassium iodide.
parts.solutionMd:
The tests that the student could do to show that the mixture contains potassium carbonate and potassium iodide are:

Descriptions to include **six **of the following points:

Potassium ion / K<sup>+</sup>:

- Flame test / description of a flame test; **[1 mark]**
- Lilac flame (seen for the potassium ion / K<sup>+</sup>); **[1 mark] **

Carbonate ion / CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup>:

- Add (any named) acid; **[1 mark]**
- Pass / bubble the gas / carbon dioxide / CO<sub>2</sub> into limewater; **[1 mark]**
- Which goes cloudy / milky / forms a white precipitate **AND **Mention of limewater in the answer; **[1 mark]**

Iodide ion / I<sup>–</sup>:

- Add silver nitrate (solution);** [1 mark]**
- A yellow precipitate / solid (is seen for the iodide ion / I<sup>–</sup>) **AND **Mention of silver nitrate in the answer;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *Make sure you know your chemical tests for the various ions along with the associated positive results*

parts.problemMd:
A technician finds a white solid in an unlabelled beaker. She knows that the solid is one of the following substances:

- potassium chloride
- potassium sulfate
- sodium chloride
- sodium sulfate.

Describe how the technician can use chemical tests to identify the solid in the beaker.
parts.solutionMd:
The technician can use chemical tests to identify the solid in the beaker:

A description that makes reference to the following six points:

Test for cation:

- Do a flame test; **[1 mark] **
- If the flame is yellow then the cation is sodium; **[1 mark]**
- If the flame is lilac then the cation is potassium;** [1 mark] **

Test for anion:

- Dissolve solid in water; **[1 mark]**

**EITHER**

- Add (dilute nitric acid and) aqueous silver nitrate;** [1 mark]**
- If a (white) precipitate forms the anion is chloride / if no precipitate forms then the anion is sulfate; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- Add (dilute hydrochloric acid and) aqueous barium chloride; **[1 mark]**
- If a (white) precipitate forms the anion is sulfate / if no precipitate forms then the anion is chloride; **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 6 marks] **

- If asked to show how different ionic compounds can be identified, break up the compounds into cations and anions

parts.problemMd:
This question is about ammonium compounds.

The table shows the names and formulae of some ammonium compounds.

| **Name** | Ammonium nitrate | Ammonium carbonate |   |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Formula** | NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> |   | NH<sub>4</sub>Cl |

i) Complete the table by giving the missing information.

(2)

ii) When ammonia reacts with nitric acid, ammonium nitrate is formed.

Write a chemical equation for this reaction.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The missing information in the table is:

- Ammonium carbonate formula = (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- NH<sub>4</sub>Cl name = ammonium chloride;** [1 mark]**

ii) The chemical equation for when ammonia reacts with nitric acid to form ammonium nitrate is:

- NH<sub>3</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The ammonium ion is NH*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*+*</sup>* *
- *The carbonate ion is CO*<sub>*3*</sub><sup>*2–*</sup>* *

  - *This means that you need two ammonium ions to balance the 2- charge from the carbonate ion*
  - *Therefore, the formula of ammonium carbonate is (NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
- *NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*Cl contains the ammonium / NH*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*+*</sup>* ion and the chloride / Cl*<sup>*–*</sup>* ion*

  - *Therefore, it is called ammonium chloride*
- *From the question, you know:*

  - *When ammonia reacts with nitric acid, ammonium nitrate is formed*
  
    - *Ammonia + nitric acid → ammonium nitrate *
  - *You are expected to know the formulae of ammonia and nitric acid*
  
    - *Ammonia = NH*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
    - *Nitric acid = HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>
  - *The formula of ammonium nitrate is NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*NO*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
  - *So, the chemical equation is:*
  
    - *NH*<sub>*3*</sub>* + HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>* → NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*NO*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
  - *No balancing is required for this equation*
  
    - *Previous exams have asked the same question using sulfuric acid to form ammonium sulfate*
    - *Although such an equation will need balancing, it was still only worth one mark! *

parts.problemMd:
When ammonium chloride is heated, it undergoes thermal decomposition to form two gaseous products.

Describe the result of testing each product with damp universal indicator paper.
parts.solutionMd:
The results for each gaseous product from the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride are:

- The products are ammonia / NH<sub>3</sub> **AND **Hydrogen chloride / HCl; **[1 mark]**
- Ammonia = (the universal indicator paper) turns blue / purple;** [1 mark]**
- Hydrogen chloride = (the universal indicator paper) turns red; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Thermal decomposition means that the ammonium chloride must be broken down, using heat, into products that can only be formed from the elements in the original ammonium chloride*

  - *You should also know that ammonium chloride is formed from the reaction of ammonia and hydrochloric acid*
  - *Therefore, you can assume that the reverse reaction is possible*
- *Ammonia is a base, which means that its gas will turn damp universal indicator paper blue / purple*
- *Hydrogen chloride is a strong acid, which means that it will turn damp universal indicator paper red*

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the apparatus used to heat ammonium chloride.

![nh4cl-thermal-decomposition-testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-modular-24-unit-2/inorganic-chemistry/chemical-tests/assets/001-nh4cl-thermal-decomposition-testing.png)

i) Suggest why the damp litmus paper is two different colours.

(1)

ii) Explain what happens to the damp litmus paper as the ammonium chloride is heated.

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The damp litmus paper is two different colours because:

- Blue litmus paper  **AND **Red litmus paper is being used;** [1 mark]**

ii) Explanation of what happens to the damp litmus paper as the ammonium chloride is heated:

- Ammonia has a lower *M*<sub>r</sub> / mass than hydrogen chloride  **AND  **Therefore, it travels **OR **diffuses quicker / faster; [**1 mark]**
- So, the (damp) red litmus paper will turn blue (first);** [1 mark]**
- The heavier / slower hydrogen chloride then turns both litmus papers red; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Remember:** Litmus paper comes in red and blue to test for alkaline and acidic chemicals respectively *
- *Using both litmus papers suggests that you will be testing for ammonia gas **AND **hydrogen chloride gas*

  - *Many students will incorrectly guess:*
  
    - *That one of the gases turns both litmus papers red / blue and the other has no effect*
    - *That the red litmus paper will turn blue and the blue litmus paper will turn red - this answer suggests that each piece of litmus paper will only be affected by the gas it should be testing for, not the other gas produced*
- *The explanation about colour changes must be linked to the difference between ammonia and hydrogen chloride*

  - *You already know that one is alkaline and the other is acidic but this does not help explain the results*
  - *Ammonia has an **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 14 + (3 x 1) = 17*
  - *Hydrogen chloride has an **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 35.5 + 1 = 36.5*
  - *This means that ammonia is lighter and can travel faster*
  - *Therefore, ammonia travels / diffuses quicker and turns the red litmus paper blue*
  - *This means that both litmus papers are blue by the time that the hydrogen chloride gets there*
  - *So, both litmus papers will then turn red*

parts.problemMd: Explain why a fine white powder formed on the inside of the neck of the conical flask in part (c).
parts.solutionMd:
A fine white powder formed on the inside of the neck of the conical flask in part (c) because:

- The ammonia and hydrogen chloride (re)formed ammonium chloride on the cooler / cold surface; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The ammonium chloride decomposes into ammonia and hydrogen chloride when heated*
- *But, ammonium chloride is formed by the reaction of ammonia and hydrogen chloride*
- *So, when the hot ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases lose energy they can react to form ammonium chloride  *

  - *Making contact with a cold surface can cause a suitable energy loss *

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the reaction between sodium and water.

Which statement about this reaction is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D.**

- When sodium reacts with water, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide are formed:

  - 2Na (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2NaOH (aq) + H<sub>2 </sub>(g)
- **A** is incorrect as sodium is less dense than water so it will float on the surface of water
- **B** is incorrect as it is potassium, not sodium, that burns with a lilac flame
- **C** is incorrect as sodium oxide is not produced in the reaction

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: Sodium sinks to the bottom of the water

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: A solution of sodium oxide is produced

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Bubbles of hydrogen gas are produced

parts.problemMd: Which of the following could **not **be predicted about caesium, based on the trends seen in Group 1 metals?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B.**

- Group 1 metals have the following physical properties

  - Low densities
  - Relatively low melting points
  - They are soft
  - They are very reactive

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: It has a relatively high melting point

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: It has a relatively low density

parts.problemMd:
A teacher adds a small piece of potassium to a large trough of water to form a solution.

When the reaction has completed she adds a few drops of universal indicator to the solution.

What is the most likely pH value of the solution?
parts.solutionMd:
**The correct answer is D**.

- When potassium reacts with water it forms potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas

  - Potassium hydroxide dissolves in water to form an alkaline solution
  - This solution will turn Universal indicator purple, showing it is strongly alkaline
  - A pH value of 12 is indicative of a strong alkali

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry Only

Sodium and rubidium have similar chemical properties because their atoms
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B.**

- The alkali metals share similar characteristic chemical properties because they each have one electron in their outer shell
- **A** is incorrect as they do form positive ions but their chemical properties are not determined by this
- **C** is incorrect as they have different numbers of electrons therefore will have different electronic configurations
- **D** is incorrect as they will lose electrons, not gain them, when they react to form positive ions

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: Have the same number of electrons in their outer shell

parts.problemMd:
This question is about some of the Group 1 alkali metals and their reactions.

i) Complete the sentence to describe a characteristic reaction of the Group 1 elements.

(2)

Group 1 elements react with ____________________ to form ____________________ solutions and hydrogen.

ii) Solid lithium reacts with cold water to form an aqueous solution of lithium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

Lithium + water → lithium hydroxide + hydrogen

Which is the correct balanced chemical equation for the reaction of lithium with water?

(1)

| ☐ | **A** | Li (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (g) → LiOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **B** | Li (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → LiOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) |
| ☐ | **C** | 2Li (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2LiOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) |
| ☐ | **D** | 2Li (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (g) → 2LiOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g) |
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed sentence is:

Group 1 elements react with **water **to form **alkaline **solutions and hydrogen.

- Water; **[1 mark]**
- Alkaline / alkali;** [1 mark]**

ii) The correct balanced chemical equation for the reaction of lithium with water is:

- **C** / 2Li (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2LiOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *For part (i)*

  - *One of the common reactions / demonstrations for Group 1 elements is the reaction with water*
  - *There is a clear pattern to their reactions with water, becoming increasingly more violent as you descend the group*
  - *However, chemically the Group 1 elements all react in a similar fashion:*
  
    - *metal + water ⟶ metal hydroxide + hydrogen *
    - *2M (s) + 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O (l) ⟶ 2MOH (aq) + H*<sub>*2*</sub>* (g)*

- *For part (ii)*

  - *From the information and your knowledge, you should know that lithium is solid (s), water is liquid (l), lithium hydroxide is an aqueous solution (aq) and hydrogen is a gas (g)*
  
    - *__Li (**s**) + __H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O (**l**) → __LiOH (**aq**) + H*<sub>*2*</sub>* (**g**)*
    - *This means that options **A** and **D** cannot be correct regardless of the balancing*
  - *Looking at the balancing of option **B**:*
  
    - *There is one lithium atom on each side of the chemical equation*
    - *There is one oxygen atom on each side of the chemical equation*
    - *However, there are two hydrogen atoms on the left-hand side and three hydrogen atoms on the right-hand side*
    - *So, option **B** is unbalanced and cannot be correct*
  - *Looking at the balancing of option **C**:*
  
    - *There are two lithium atoms on each side of the chemical equation*
    - *There are two oxygen atoms on each side of the chemical equation*
    - *There are four hydrogen atoms on each side of the chemical equation*
    - *So, option **C** is balanced and the correct answer*

parts.problemMd:
Place the following Group 1 metals in order from least to most reactive.

- Caesium
- Lithium
- Potassium
- Sodium

| **least reactive ** |   |   |   |   |   | **most reactive** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| _______________ | → | _______________ | → | _______________ | → | _______________ |
parts.solutionMd:
The order of the Group 1 metals from most to least reactive is:

| **least reactive ** |   |   |   |   |   | **most reactive** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| lithium | → | sodium | → | potassium | → | caesium |

- Lithium identified as the least reactive; [1 mark]
- Caesium identified as the most reactive;** [1 mark]**
- Sodium and potassium placed in the correct order; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The Group 1 metals / elements get more reactive as you move down the group*
- *Using the Periodic Table, the order of the Group 1 elements from the top to the bottom of the group is:*

  - *Lithium*
  - *Sodium*
  - *Potassium*
  - *Rubidium*
  - *Caesium*
  - *Francium*
- *Removing rubidium and francium from this list gives you the correct order of the Group 1 metals / elements from least to most reactive*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry Only

i)The chemical symbol for the Group 1 metal sodium is ${}_{11}^{23}{Na}$.

State the number of electrons in one atom of sodium.

(1)

ii) Complete the diagram to show the arrangement of electrons in a sodium atom.

(2)

![3-blank-electron-shells](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-modular-24-unit-2/inorganic-chemistry/group-1/assets/006-3-blank-electron-shells.png)

iii) Group 1 metals like sodium typically form ionic compounds with other elements.

State how a Group 1 metal atom, M, becomes a Group 1 metal ion, M<sup>+</sup>.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The number of electrons in one atom of sodium is:

- 11 / eleven; **[1 mark] **

ii) The completed diagram to show the arrangement of electrons in a sodium atom is:

- One electron on the outer shell;** [1 mark]**
- Eight electrons on the middle shell **AND **Two electrons on the inner shell; **[1 mark]**

iii) A Group1 metal atom becomes a Group 1 metal ion by:

- Losing <u>one</u> electron;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *For part (i)*

  - *The smaller number on the chemical symbol of an element is the atomic or proton number*
  - *The question asks about an atom, which means that the number of protons = the number of electrons *
  - *Therefore, sodium has 11 electrons *
- *For part (ii)*

  - *Sodium is on the third row of the Periodic Table, which is why it has three electron shells*
  
    - *The first row / period of the Periodic Table has two elements *
    
      - *The first / inner shell of electrons can hold a maximum of 2 electrons*
    - *The second row / period of the Periodic Table has eight elements *
    
      - *The second shell of electrons can hold a maximum of 8 electrons*
    - *The third row / period of the Periodic Table has eight elements *
    
      - *The third shell of electrons can hold a maximum of 8 electrons*
  - *Using this information, you can determine that sodium has 2 electrons on the inner shell, 8 electrons on the middle shell and 1 electron on the outer shell*
- *For part (iii)*

  - *Group 1 metals have one negative electron in their outer shell*
  - *When they lose this one negative outer electron, they become an ion (charged particle) with a 1+ charge*
  - *This can also be shown using an equation:*
  
    - *M → M*<sup>*+*</sup>* + e*<sup>*–*</sup>* *

parts.problemMd:
Explain why francium is more reactive than rubidium.

Use the words in the boxes to complete the sentences. Each word may be used once, more than once or not at all.

| greater | electrostatic | weaker |
|---|---|---|
| stronger | less | thermal |

The distance between the outermost electron of francium and its nucleus is __________ than that of rubidium.

This means that the forces of attraction in francium are __________ .

Therefore, __________ energy is required to overcome the forces of attraction in francium.
parts.solutionMd:
The completed sentences to explain why francium is more reactive than rubidium are:

| greater | electrostatic | weaker |
|---|---|---|
| stronger | less | thermal |

- The distance between the outermost electron of francium and its nucleus is **greater **than that of rubidium;** [1 mark]**
- This means that the forces of attraction in francium are **weaker OR less**; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, **less **energy is required to overcome the forces of attraction in francium; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Sentence 1 is comparing francium and rubidium*

  - *This means that the possible answers are greater, stronger, weaker or less*
  - *Francium is at the bottom of Group 1, which means that it is the largest Group 1 atom and must have the greatest distance from its nucleus to the outermost electron*
- *Sentence 2 is inversely linked to sentence 1*

  - *The greater the distance from the nucleus to the outermost electron, the weaker the force of attraction *
  - *Careful:** The word electrostatic is a distraction because it is an electrostatic force of attraction between the nucleus of an atom and its outermost electron, but this is true for all elements *
- *Sentence 3 is directly linked to sentence 2*

  - *Weaker forces of attraction require less energy to overcome*
  - *Careful:** The word thermal is a distraction because it is a type of energy*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the elements in Group 1 of the Periodic Table and their reactions with water.

State why sodium and potassium are in Group 1 of the Periodic Table.
parts.solutionMd:
Sodium and potassium are in Group 1 of the Periodic Table because:

- The atoms of both elements have one electron in the outer shell / highest energy level; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The number of electrons in the outer shell is the same as the group number in the Periodic Table*

  - *If there is 1 electron in the outer shell, the element is in Group 1, as is the case with both sodium and potassium*

parts.problemMd:
A reaction occurs when a small piece of sodium is added to a large volume of water in a trough.

i) Give **two** observations that you would make during this reaction.

(2)

ii) After the reaction has finished, a few drops of universal indicator are added to the solution in the trough. Explain the final colour of the universal indicator.

(2)

iii) What is the most likely pH value of the solution in the trough after the reaction is complete?

| ☐ | **A** | 2 |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **B** | 5 |
| ☐ | **C** | 8 |
| ☐ | **D** | 12 |

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) **Two** observations that you would make during this reaction are:

A description that makes reference to any **two** of the following points:

- Sodium floats / moves across the water;** [1 mark]**
- Sodium melts; **[1 mark] **
- Sodium disappears / gets smaller;** [1 mark] **
- Effervescence / fizzing / bubbles / gas given off; **[1 mark] **
- White trail; **[1 mark] **

ii) The final colour of the universal indicator is:

- (Final colour is) purple / blue; **[1 mark] **
- Because the solution is alkaline; **[1 mark] **

iii) The most likely pH value of the solution in the trough is:

- **D** / 12; **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 5 marks] **

- *You should know the observations for when a Group 1 metal reacts with water*
- *The reaction becomes more violent down the group*

  - *This is a common demonstration and you may remember the metal floating and whizzing around the trough *

parts.problemMd: Give the name of a Group 1 metal that is less reactive than sodium.
parts.solutionMd:
A Group 1 metal that is less reactive than sodium is:

- Lithium / Li; **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 1 mark] **

- *The Group 1 metals become more reactive as you go down the group*
- *Therefore the only metal that is less reactive than sodium in Group 1 will be lithium *

parts.problemMd: A small piece of potassium is added to a large volume of water in a trough. Give **one **observation that is made when potassium is added to water that is not made when sodium is added to water.
parts.solutionMd:
The extra observation for potassium is:

- Catches fire **OR **Produces a lilac / purple / violet flame; **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 1 mark] **

- *The flame colour of potassium is a characteristic lilac colour *
- *The reaction of potassium and water is more exothermic than that of sodium or lithium*
- *Therefore, there is enough heat to ignite the hydrogen gas given off*
- *This burns and, due to the potassium ions present, a lilac flame is seen *

parts.problemMd:
Complete the equation for the reaction of rubidium with water. State symbols are not required.

........Rb + ........H<sub>2</sub>O → ........RbOH + .........H<sub>2</sub>
parts.solutionMd:
The completed equation is:

- **2**(Rb + ) **2*****(***H<sub>2</sub>O →) **2**(RbOH + H<sub>2</sub>); **[1 mark]** *Accept multiples and fractions*

**[Total: 1 mark] **

- *This is an equation that you do not need to know, you just need to know the general equation for the reaction between Group 1 metals and water and oxygen*
- *If the Group 1 metal is M then*

  - *Reaction with **oxygen**:*
  
    - *2M + ½O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → M*<sub>*2*</sub>*O  OR*
    - *4**M + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**M*<sub>*2*</sub>*O *
  - *Reaction with **water**:*

- *If a chemical / substance has a high melting point, then it will require a large amount of energy to break bonds or overcome forces of attraction*

Explain why potassium is more reactive than lithium.

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
i) One observation that would be different if potassium is used instead of lithium is:

Any **one **from:

- More rapid bubbles / fizzing / effervescence;** [1 mark]**
- Melts / turns into a ball;  **[1 mark]**
- Moves more quickly; ** [1 mark]**
- Gets smaller more quickly;  **[1 mark]**
- Catches alight / burns / produces a flame; **[1 mark]**

ii) Potassium is more reactive than lithium because:

- Potassium has more shells / is bigger than lithium **OR **The outer shell / electron in potassium is further from the nucleus;  **[1 mark]**
- (Therefore) there is less attraction between the outer shell/electron and the nucleus **OR **There is more repulsion (from inner shells) **OR **There is more shielding (from the nuclear attraction) **OR **The nuclear pull for the outer shell / electron is weaker;** [1 mark]**
- So the electron in the outer shell is more easily lost; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *For part (ii), the reverse argument for lithium will also score the marks*
- *Potassium is further down Group 1, so has a more vigorous reaction than lithium*
- *Make sure your answer is comparative, for example, it moves **more **quickly, not just it moves *
- *Group 1 reactivity is determined by how easily the element loses its outer electron to form a positive ion *
- *The further away the negative outer electron is from the positive nucleus, the weaker the attraction is and the more easily the electron is lost*
- *This is a common explanation you will be asked about, so make sure you learn the three points*

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry Only

The equation for the reaction between lithium and water is:

2Li (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2LiOH (aq) + H<sub>2 </sub>(g)

i) A mass of 0.500 g of lithium reacts with an excess of water. Calculate the volume, in cm<sup>3</sup>, of hydrogen gas produced at rtp.

[molar volume of a gas at rtp = 24 000 cm<sup>3</sup>]

Give your answer to three significant figures.

(3)

volume = .......................................... cm<sup>3</sup>

ii) In a reaction between lithium and water, 150 cm<sup>3</sup> of lithium hydroxide solution is formed.

The lithium hydroxide solution is then completely neutralised by 24.85 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.100 mol/dm<sup>3</sup> sulfuric acid. The equation for the neutralisation is

2LiOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(aq) → Li<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Calculate the concentration, in mol/dm<sup>3</sup>, of the lithium hydroxide solution.

(3)

concentration = .............................................................. mol/dm<sup>3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
i) The volume, in cm<sup>3</sup>, of hydrogen gas produced at rtp is:

- Moles of Li= $\frac{0.500}{7}$ **OR** 0.0714;** [1 mark]**
- Moles of H<sub>2</sub>=$\frac{0.0714}{2}$ **OR** 0.0357; **[1 mark]**
- Volume of H<sub>2</sub> (= 0.0357 x 24000) = 857 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

ii) The concentration, in mol/dm<sup>3</sup>, of the lithium hydroxide solution is:

- Moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>= 0.02485 x 0.1 **OR** 0.002485;** [1 mark]**
- Moles of LiOH = 2 x 0.002485 **OR **0.00497; **[1 mark]**
- Concentration of LiOH = 0.0331 (mol/dm<sup>3</sup>);** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *To calculate the volume of gas *

  - *Find the number of moles of lithium using* $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{mass}}$
  - *The molar ratio of lithium to hydrogen gas is 2:1 so divide the number of moles of lithium by 2*
  - *Multiply the number of moles of hydrogen by 24 000 to find the volume it occupies *
  - *Make sure your answer is to three significant figures!*
- *To calculate the concentration of lithium hydroxide*

  - *You are able to calculate the moles of sulfuric acid using concentration x volume (making sure you have converted volume from cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* to dm*<sup>*3*</sup>*) so 0.02485 x 0.1 = 0.002485 mol*
  - *The equation tells you that the molar ratio of lithium hydroxide to sulfuric acid is 2:1 so you need to multiply the moles of sulfuric acid by 2 to give 0.00497 mol*
  - *Concentration can be found by using *$\frac{\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{moles}}{\mathrm{volume}}$ *so *$\frac{0.00497}{0.150}$*=  0.0331 mol / dm*<sup>*3*</sup>

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry Only

i) Give the balanced chemical equation for the reaction of potassium with hydrochloric acid. State symbols are required.

(2)

ii) Draw diagrams to show the arrangement of the electrons in the product of this reaction.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The balanced chemical equation including state symbols for the reaction of potassium with hydrochloric acid is:

2K (s) + 2HCl (aq) → 2KCl (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g)

- Correct chemical formulae **AND **Correct state symbols; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

ii) The diagrams to show the arrangement of the electrons in the product of this reaction are:

- Correct electron arrangement of the potassium ion  **AND **Correct electron arrangement of the chloride ion; **[1 mark]**
- Correct charges on <u>both</u> ions; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *For part (i)*

  - *The reaction of potassium with hydrochloric acid is: Potassium + hydrochloric acid → potassium chloride + hydrogen*
  
    - *Potassium = K (s)*
    - *Hydrochloric acid = HCl (aq)*
    - *Potassium chloride = KCl (aq)*
    - *Hydrogen = H*<sub>*2*</sub>* (g)*
  - *This gives the unbalanced chemical equation:*
  
    - *K (s) + HCl (aq) → KCl (aq) + H*<sub>*2*</sub>* (g)*
  - *There are two hydrogen atoms on the right-hand side, so you need 2HCl on the left-hand side*
  
    - *K (s) + **2**HCl (aq) → KCl (aq) + H*<sub>*2*</sub>* (g)*
  - *There are now two chlorine atoms on the left-hand side, so you need 2KCl on the right-hand side*
  
    - *K (s) + **2**HCl (aq) → **2**KCl (aq) + H*<sub>*2*</sub>* (g)*
  - *There are now two potassium atoms on the right-hand side, so you need 2K on the left-hand side*
  
    - *2**K (s) + **2**HCl (aq) → **2**KCl (aq) + H*<sub>*2*</sub>* (g)*
- *For part (ii)*

  - *Careful:** The question asks for the arrangement of the electrons in the product*
  
    - *This means that you need to draw how the electrons are arranged in the potassium and chloride ions that form potassium chloride*
    - *A common mistake is to draw how the electrons are arranged in **atoms** of potassium and chlorine*
  - *Unless you are told otherwise, the arrangement of electrons in an ion should include the electrons in the inner shells *
  - *The potassium ion and chloride ion have the same arrangement of electrons which is why they are both required for the mark to awarded*
  
    - *If the metal ion and non-metal ion had different electron arrangements, there would be one mark for the metal ion diagram and one mark for the non-metal ion diagram*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about some Group 1 metal oxides.

When lithium is exposed to oxygen, it is oxidised and traces of lithium peroxides are produced.

i) Explain why the formation of lithium oxide is a redox reaction.

(3)

ii) Lithium oxide and a gas are produced by the thermal decomposition of lithium peroxide, Li<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

Write the balanced chemical equation for this reaction. State symbols are not required.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The formation of lithium oxide from lithium and oxygen is a redox reaction because:

- Lithium is oxidised **AND **oxygen is reduced **OR **Both oxidation and reduction occur;** [1 mark]**
- Lithium gains oxygen **OR **Lithium loses electrons **OR **The oxidation number of lithium increases / changes from 0 to +1; **[1 mark]**
- Oxygen gains electrons  **OR **The oxidation number of oxygen decreases from 0 to –2; **[1 mark]**

ii) The balanced chemical equation for the production of lithium oxide and a gas by the thermal decomposition of lithium peroxide, Li<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is:

2Li<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → 2Li<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>

- Correct chemical formulae; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Redox reactions can be considered in terms of:*

  - *Oxygen *
  
    - *Oxidation is the gain of oxygen, which is what happens to the lithium*
    - *Reduction is the loss of oxygen, but this does not work for this reaction*
  - *Electrons (OILRIG)*
  
    - *Oxidation is the loss of electrons*
    
      - *The lithium loses one electron to become the Li*<sup>*+*</sup>* ion required to form lithium oxide*
    - *Reduction is the gain of electrons*
    
      - *Each oxygen atom gains 2 electrons to become the O*<sup>*2-*</sup>* ion required to form lithium oxide*
  - *Answers in terms of oxidation number are accepted although these are considered above the level of this course*
- *You are told that lithium peroxide decomposes to form lithium oxide and a gas*

  - *The gas must be oxygen, which gives the unbalanced equation:*
  
    - *Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
  - *To get an even number of oxygen atoms on the right-hand side, you double the lithium oxide:*
  
    - *Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
  - *There are now four lithium atoms and four oxygen atoms on the right-hand side, so you double the lithium peroxide*
  
    - *2**Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
  - *The equation is now balanced*

parts.problemMd:
The oxidation of potassium can produce potassium oxide, K<sub>2</sub>O, and potassium superoxide, KO<sub>2</sub>.

Compare the oxidation of potassium with the combustion of carbon.
parts.solutionMd:
Comparing the oxidation of potassium with the combustion of carbon:

- Potassium reacts in excess oxygen / a plentiful supply of oxygen to form potassium superoxide / KO<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- This is similar to the complete combustion of carbon to form carbon dioxide / CO<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Potassium reacts in limited oxygen to form potassium oxide / K<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**
- This is similar to the incomplete combustion of carbon to form carbon monoxide / CO; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Answers in terms of carbon reacting with excess or limited oxygen and then the equivalent comparison to the oxidations of potassium will score the marks*
- *There are two oxidation of potassium reactions given in the question *

  - *Potassium + oxygen → potassium superoxide K + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
  - *Potassium + oxygen → potassium oxide 4K + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2K*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Carbon can undergo complete and incomplete combustion*

  - *Complete combustion Carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide C + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *Incomplete combustion Carbon + oxygen → carbon monoxide 2C + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2CO*
- *The formation of potassium superoxide and the complete combustion of carbon both have one mole of reactant (potassium or carbon) reacting with one mole of oxygen to form the oxide*

  - *This suggests that they both require a plentiful supply of oxygen*
- *The formation of potassium oxide and the incomplete combustion of carbon both have multiple moles of reactant (potassium or carbon) reacting with one mole of oxygen to form the oxide*

  - *This suggests that they both have a limited supply of oxygen*

parts.problemMd:
Potassium superoxide is sometimes used as a water dehumidifier, carbon dioxide scrubber and oxygen generator on board space craft and submarines.

As it absorbs and reacts with carbon dioxide, it locks the carbon dioxide up as potassium carbonate and releases oxygen.

i) Write the balanced chemical equation for this chemical reaction. State symbols are not required.

(2)

ii) Determine the number of moles of carbon dioxide absorbed and the number of moles of oxygen released by one mole of potassium superoxide.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The balanced chemical equation for potassium superoxide locking carbon dioxide up as potassium carbonate and releasing oxygen is:

4KO<sub>2</sub> + 2CO<sub>2</sub> → 2K<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + 3O<sub>2</sub>

- Correct chemical formulae; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing;** [1 mark] **

ii) The number of moles of carbon dioxide absorbed and the number of moles of oxygen released by one mole of potassium superoxide are:

- Carbon dioxide absorbed = 0.5 moles; **[1 mark]**
- Oxygen released = 0.75 moles; [1 mark]

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *When potassium superoxide absorbs and reacts with carbon dioxide, it locks it up in the form of potassium carbonate*

  - *This is similar to carbon dioxide from the early atmosphere that was locked up in calcium carbonate *
- *The unbalanced chemical equation is:*

  - *KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
- *The three oxygen atoms in potassium carbonate make balancing the equation more challenging as there is an even number of oxygen atoms on the left-hand side*

  - *This can be resolved by producing 2K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
  
    - *KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
- *This means that there are four potassium atoms on the right-hand side and only one potassium atom on the left-hand side*

  - *This can be resolved by using 4KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
  - *4**KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
- *There are also two carbon atoms on the right-hand side and only one carbon atom on the left-hand side*

  - *This can be resolved by using 2CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
  - *4**KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **2**CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
- *There are now 12 oxygen atoms on the left-hand side*

  - *There are six oxygen atoms in the 2K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>*, which leave 6 oxygen atoms*
  - *This imbalance can be resolved by producing 3O*<sub>*2*</sub>*  *
  - *4**KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **2**CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + **3**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
- *To determine the number of moles of carbon dioxide absorbed and the number of moles of oxygen released, you can use your chemical equation*

  - *4KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + 3O*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
  - *4 moles of potassium superoxide react with 2 moles of carbon dioxide*
  
    - *Therefore, 1 mole of potassium superoxide will react with *$\frac{2}{4}$* or 0.5 moles of carbon dioxide*
  - *4 moles of potassium superoxide produce 3 moles of oxygen*
  
    - *Therefore, 1 mole of potassium superoxide will produce *$\frac{3}{4}$* or 0.75 moles of oxygen*

ii) State why the teacher does not add bromine solution to sodium bromide solution.

(1)

iii) The word equation for the reaction of bromine with sodium iodide is

(1)
parts.solutionMd:

| ** bromine solution** | solution stays orange | not done | solution turns brown |
| ** iodine solution** | **(solution stays) brown / no change / no reaction**; **[1 mark]** | solution stays brown | not done |

ii) The teacher does not add bromine solution to sodium bromide solution because:

- Bromine would not react with (sodium) bromide / bromine cannot displace itself / cannot react with itself **OR **Both solutions contain bromine / the same element / the same halogen **OR **No reaction would take place; **[1 mark] **
